speechtext:
It is
ilways a pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to welcome he motion introduced annually by the Secreary of State for External Affairs (Mr. 3earson) to refer the estimates of his depart-nent to the standing committee on external iffairs. I have always regarded that as a rery healthy procedure, and one that has ed to a wider measure of participation in he discussion of external affairs as well as, I think, a broader understanding of the

problems of external affairs on the part of members of this house than would otherwise be possible. The committee, under the able and benevolent chairmanship of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), is one to which all members regard it as a pleasure to belong, and to participate in its discussions.
The extent of the review of Canada's external relations by the minister yesterday and today, as well as the breadth and scope of the speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), stressed and underlined the extent to which Canada is interested in virtually all that takes place in all parts of the globe. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said in some speeches last summer that today it is virtually impossible for Canada not to become involved in a major war, should one break out. It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that the course of Canada's interest in world affairs and the extent of her commitments in various theatres of the world have led to the result that when we debate external affairs in this house we range virtually over the entire globe.
The world situation today seems to be, at least through the eyes of the west, a matter of balancing strength against dangers, of pitting the resources of the free western world against the needs. The resources are still not adequate to meet the needs. As Mr. Churchill said several years ago, to attempt to be strong everywhere is to be strong nowhere. We hope we are moving in the direction of increasing our strength so that in time the strength of the free western world may be reasonably adequate to meet the challenge of our needs. As yet we are far from having reached the point where our strength is adequate to meet that challenge.
It is important, in the first place, that we should recognize the nature and source of the danger. Literally there is one primary source and only one, and that, of course, is the Kremlin with its policies of world domination. We ought to recognize that danger for what it is, naked, unabashed aggression; a cold, calculating, ruthless attempt to subvert freedom the whole world over. The Kremlin is deaf to all appeals to honour and to humane considerations. I do not think we are going to come very much closer to a satisfactory solution in Korea or in any of the other troubled parts of the world today by thinking we can discuss this matter in terms of appeals to humane considerations or honour on the part of those against whom we are pitted in this cold war. Wishful thinking is going to do us no good in influencing those against whose aggressive intent we are in process of becoming arrayed. They just do not think our way. Their thought processes are entirely different from ours.

We should recognize also that what we see unfolding today is a world plan. Lightning may be striking in different parts of the world, but when the lightning of communism strikes today it is part of a world-wide plan, whether it be armed aggression in Korea; armed aggression in Indo-China, Burma, Malaya; the cold war in other parts of the world; persecution of Jewish leaders in the European countries behind the iron curtain, or the severing of diplomatic relations with the state of Israel with a view to stirring up trouble in the Arab world. These are all facets of the unfolding world plan of aggression directed from the Kremlin.
Of course the advantage of a single direction of a world plan lies with the communists, as well as the advantage of the initiative. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I think we will have accomplished something in the western world if we do recognize the nature and source of this danger and then gird ourselves to meet it.
Beneficent international institutions seem to develop slowly. That seems to be one of the characteristics of such institutions. The United Nations, NATO, the point four plan, the Marshall plan, the Schuman plan, the policy of containment-these all have been characterized by slow growth. That is not to say that their growth has lacked strength because it was slow; nevertheless it seems to be a characteristic of international institutions of the beneficent type.
What may be said to be the focal points of danger today? What is the need of the western world where the pressure of communist aggression is strongest? It seems to me, sir, that whether you look at Europe or whether you look at Asia, the danger is extremely grave today. I suppose in Asia our answer to the threat and the present dangers there will lie in our hope of resisting armed aggression in Korea and in the countries of southeast Asia, in strengthening a friendly Japan, and in our hope that India, great country that she is, will see her way clear in the days that lie before us to take a clearer and stronger line in recognizing and confronting the communist menace in Asia.
In Europe the need for unity of the western nations is extremely urgent. It is because of the importance of strength in western Europe, and in particular the need for a stronger measure of unity between France and Germany, that I should like to share with the house some impressions that it was my privilege to form during a visit to western Europe last October. This offered an opportunity to measure the developments in western Europe in the four years since one had had a previous opportunity, along with
External Affairs
certain members of this house, to visit th principal countries of western Europe.
Western Europe is making a strong come back. Let no one underestimate the exten of the economic comeback of western Europe Western Germany today has a greater pro duction than the entire pre-war Hitler Ger many. France today has a greater productioi than pre-war France. Britain today has ; greater production than pre-war Britair These are all factors of high importance ii balancing the scales against the threat o Soviet aggression. Our economic resources ar in pawn, Mr. Speaker, in this world struggl just as much as is our military migh expressed in terms of rearmament.

I should like to say a word about the vexed question of German rearmament, based upon discussions which it was my privilege to have with some of the leading political figures in Britain, as well as in Paris and Germany.
I suppose if the Russians had not behaved as they have since the war no one would feel happy about the prospect of German rearmament. The experience we have had with an armed Germany led by the German general staff has not been such as to create in us any feeling of confidence or satisfaction over the prospect of German rearmament. Nevertheless some hard facts have emerged which it is no longer possible to overlook.
The load the British taxpayer is carrying and the drain upon British manpower, not only in the army of the Rhine but in the discharge of Britain's obligations all over the world, is so great that when the Britisher looks at Germany and sees British forces garrisoning Western Germany, sees that Germany has not yet been called upon to bear her share of the burden and responsibility of rearming, is it any wonder that he says, "Why is not Germany carrying her share of this load?"
France is weighed down with her struggles and her burdens. There is a continual drain on her resources because of the war in Indochina. But she looks at Germany with a different feeling because the recollection of three German invasions in the last 80 years is still very fresh in the minds of her people.
It is easy enough for us at this safe distance to make plans for western Europe, but it is not going to be an easy matter to fuse German, French and forces of other countries in western Europe into a European army. If it comes about, as we may well hope that in some form it will, it will be indeed a triumph of statesmanship and abundant evidence that we have entered upon a new era of co-operation and understanding.

The nationalist tradition is still very strong In the French army. Nationalism is still strong in France. The distrust of Germany in the light of the experience of the last 80 years is still strong.
It was the United States that first put forward the proposal for German rearmament because today Western Germany with a population of fifty million has the greatest available pool of manpower in western Europe. Mr. Schuman brought forward the idea of a European army with smaller German units fitted into it, as a compromise plan. That became the Schuman plan in regard to a European army. But a European army built upon the fusion of smaller units drawn from various countries is very different from a force built up of component national armies of various countries and serving under a supreme commander, such as we had in the latter part of the first great war and throughout most of the second world war.
Therefore we should not underestimate the difficulties that the nations of western Europe are facing in relation to this matter of German rearmament as part of the formation of a European army. It is to be hoped that something of that kind will come about, because except from a greater measure of unity in western Europe we may look in vain for that revival of strength in Europe, drawn from European sources, which is so necessary today in the face of the strength that Russia is mustering behind the iron curtain and in face of the political difficulties that exist at Washington in connection with the maintenance and continuance of United States aid.
Back of all this, Mr. Speaker, stands Britain-Britain which has carried such a burden, Britain which has undergone such privations not simply for her survival but for the peace and deliverance of all mankind. I hope that when people call upon Britain to carry a greater share of the load of the world's problems they will not forget what that land suffered during the war, the burden that land carried during the war and since. They are still bearing privations that are matched by few of the countries that enjoy today that measure of freedom and deliverance which Britain made such sacrifices to help win for them. Make no mistake about it, people have been writing Britain off for generations as though her best days were behind her. I am here, Mr. Speaker, to bear testimony to my belief that the best days of Britain lie before her, that no nation that has been called upon to fulfil the beneficent destiny for all mankind and for the freedom of mankind that Britain has been called upon to fulfil could fail in days like these.

Surely this all adds up to the fact that a major war is going on at the present time.
The policy of containment, the policy of neutralizing the war or attempting to isolate the war, has certainly failed. We are now adopting, or the United States is adopting, a more realistic attitude toward the situation.
I want to mention briefly the situation in Europe. I was privileged to spend about a month behind the iron curtain, not only in East Germany and in Austria, but in two of the satellite countries. The feeling in the satellite countries is such that there are literally millions of people in Europe hoping for war because by war they stand their only chance of liberation from their Russian masters.

There is no question about it; when the German troops went into the Ukraine they were met with garlands as deliverers. That feeling still exists. When we say that we are fighting a purely limited war, what encouragement does that give to these people behind the iron curtain? What encouragement does it give to the people of the Ukraine, who have the dream that some day there will be a free Ukrainian state? What encouragement does it give to the people of Poland, of Czechoslovakia or of Hungary, who have the dream that again they will be free? It gives them no encouragement.
I saw enough to know that one of the reasons Russia did not attack when she was prepared in 1947 was that she was not sure of her people. Well, Mr. Speaker, she was not sure then and she is very much less sure of them now. We have to encourage those people, and we have to encourage them by our policy. A policy of restricted action, of containment, of an isolated war is something that does not bring them encouragement. They want to be free; they want to get out from under the yoke of communism. Just as we are fighting communism, so they want to fight communism.
If there is proof needed of that, look at the purges that are now going on. There is not any satellite country today that has had a continuing communist hierarchy which has lasted for over a year. Surely that shows the conditions of unrest which exist. I think there is a very direct connection between the alliance or the joint action taken by Greece, Turkey and Yugoslavia in the Balkans. I am sure that the impact of this anti-cominform pact on countries like Bulgaria, Albania and even Roumania is certainly very considerable. Now, are we going to encourage that? Are we going to encourage an attack there on the flank? Of course we are. Why, then, should we not encourage an attack on the other flank in China? There are many ways of beating the communists, and we have to use all of them.
Let us not try to play a safe war. There is no such thing as a safe war, and to attempt to play it that way is the surest way to national suicide. We have to be prepared in our minds to realize that there is no such thing as a safe war.
One last problem we have to meet is the problem of German refugees. Today there are about 1,000 refugees fleeing East Germany every day. They get over the frontier and come into Berlin in different ways, and they impose a tremendous problem of housing and overcrowding, not only in Berlin but in the whole West German state. This overcrowding and this apparent lack of interest

on our part in these refugees is in my opinion

and I spent some time in Germany- one of the contributing causes of the rise of neo-nazism. I heard it said over and over again: America and Canada are not interested in us because they won't do anything about this overcrowding.
I feel that one of the things that must be done if we are going to have stability in the West German government and if we are going to prevent the rise of neo-nazism is to see that something is done about the problem of the German refugee fleeing from the communists in East Germany.
